en: Now, therefore, we shall explain the domestic rites (gṛhyakarmāṇi).

1. The ritual must be performed by one wearing the sacrificial cord (yajñopavītin) and having sipped water (ācāntodaka). 2. One should know that the proper time for [the rites] is during the northern course of the sun (udagayana), in the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa), on an auspicious day, before the turning point of the day. 3.
And according to the specific instruction,
all [rites] indeed involve the *anvāhārya* (subsidiary fee);
at the conclusion, there is a meal for worthy persons according to one's ability.

A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), having studied the Veda, when about to place the final fuel-stick on the fire (7), or when desiring to take the hand of his wife (8), shall fetch water that has been well-protected. Having swept a place that slopes toward the northeast or is level, and having smeared it with cow-dung, he shall draw a line from west to east in the middle, and a continuous line from south to north behind it; then, having drawn three lines from west to east in the middle, he shall sprinkle them with water. (9)
This [method] is everywhere according to the indicative sense (*lakṣaṇā*). 10.
They lead the fire forward while facing it with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. 11.
Or, when the master of the house has died, the performance of the *parameṣṭhin* rite takes place. 12.
Likewise, when there is a conjunction of the lunar day, the asterism, and the festival—
on either the new moon or the full moon— he should establish the sacred fire;
he should fetch the fire from the house of a Vaiśya or from an ambarīṣa fire-vessel and place it upon the altar.
Or rather, he may take it from the house of a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya who performs many sacrifices; or he may kindle another fire by friction and add it to the sacred fire;
for thus the fire becomes meritorious and not barren.
One may do as one desires. 19.
When he places the very last fuel-stick on the fire, or when he wishes to take his wife's hand and offers an oblation, he should restrain that [fire]; 20.
that indeed becomes his domestic (gṛhya) fire. 21.
"And by that very act, his morning oblation becomes offered.

22. From this point forward, the performance of the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the domestic fire is prescribed beginning with the evening oblation. 23. Before the time for the lighting of the fires, one should fetch water protected [from impurities] for the purpose of the evening and morning service. 24.
Or else, he may take [the water] from a jar or from a water-pot (maṇika) in the evening;
having kindled the fire before sunset, he should offer the evening oblation after sunset.
Before sunrise in the morning, having made the sacred fires manifest, one should offer the morning oblation either when the sun has risen or before it has risen.
(28) One puts on the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), which may be a cord, a cloth, or even a rope of *kuśa* grass.

Having raised the right arm and placed it over the head, one settles it upon the left shoulder; it hangs down along the right armpit, and in this way one becomes one who wears the sacrificial thread. (2–3)

Raising his left arm and placing it upon his head, he establishes it on his right side; thus, letting it hang down along his left armpit, he becomes one who wears the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).
Indeed, in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), he must wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder.
Having stepped away from the fire toward the north, having washed his hands and feet, and having sat down, he should sip water three times and wipe his lips twice.
Having sprinkled water on his feet, he should sprinkle his head;
he should touch the sense organs with water—
namely, the eyes, the nostrils, and the ears.
Whatever one might intend to touch, that should be touched with water.
Regarding this, they say:
"One should not touch water while walking."
Not standing, not laughing, and not looking about.
Not with [the hand] not bent, 15 not with the fingers [joined], 16 nor by an improper part [of the hand]. 17
Not making noise (18), not without looking (19),
nor outside (20).
Having imagined that a portion of his lower garment is his upper garment; 21. not with hot water; 22.
not with frothy water; 23.
And he should not go anywhere wearing sandals (24), nor with his upper garment tucked up (25), nor with a rope tied around his neck (26).
And one should not stretch out one's feet; 27.
finally, having sipped water, one becomes pure; 28.
however, one should sip water so that it touches the heart. 29.
"Otherwise, one indeed remains impure from that [act].
(30) Now, the rules for rinsing the mouth:
(31) Having slept, eaten, sneezed, bathed, drunk, changed clothes, stepped onto a road, or visited a cemetery, one who has already rinsed his mouth must rinse again. (32)
Having kindled the fire and swept around it, with his right knee bent, he should pour out a handful of water to the south of the fire with the words, "O Aditi, give your consent!
(1); to the west with the words, "O Anumati, give your consent! (2); and to the north with the words, "O Sarasvatī, give your consent! (3).
Saying, "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]," he should sprinkle water around the fire, either once or thrice, moving from left to right.
While sprinkling, he should shift the water-streams so as not to cross them, pouring toward the oblation-vessel.
Then he should offer into the fire an oblation of sacrificial food, whether it has been prepared or unprepared.
If it has not been prepared, one should wash it, sprinkle it with water, and offer it;
likewise if it is curd, milk, or gruel, using either the ladle, the vessel for the sacrificial porridge, or even the dipping-spoon.
"To Agni, svāhā!"—with this he offers the first oblation, the second silently, in the middle, and in the north-eastern direction; thus at evening.

Then in the morning, having offered a fuel-stick in the eastern direction with the formula "Svāhā to Sūrya," and the next one silently in the middle and in the north-eastern (aparājita) direction; having sprinkled water around [the fire] and poured out handfuls of water in the same manner, the specific mantra is "anvamam sthā" (follow me, ye waters). Having circumambulated the fire clockwise, having poured out the remainder of the water, and having filled and set down the cup, he may proceed as he pleases.
Thus, from this point forward, he should offer oblations himself in the domestic fire, or have them offered, until the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at the end of his life.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"The wife may, if she wishes, perform the morning and evening offerings in the domestic fire; for the house is the wife, and this fire belongs to the domestic fire."
When the evening and morning meals are finished, he should cause [the teacher] to announce, "It has been done.
(16) Having become pure, he should do so with speech that is not harsh. (17) He responds aloud, "Om," and in a low voice, "Homage to him; may he declare it to me. (18)
Alternatively, he should carry out the offerings while remaining silent;
he may speak when the food is prepared, and he may converse with guests at will.
Then, having set aside some of the sacrificial food and having sprinkled it with sacrificial condiments, he should offer it into the fire silently with his hand alone.
The first oblation belongs to Prajāpati; the second belongs to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Then he should carry forth the Bali offerings, having prepared a good spot of ground, either outside or inside [the house].
Having poured water once, he should place the Bali in four parts, and finally he should sprinkle water around it once.
One should sprinkle water around each individual offering on both sides.

That which he places first becomes the offering to Earth; that which is second is for Vāyu; that which is third is for the Viśvedevas; and that which is fourth is for Prajāpati. Then he should carry forth other offerings: at the middle door of the water-vessel, the first offering is for the Waters; the second is for the Plants and Trees; the third is for Space.
Now, furthermore, if one should offer an oblation on the bed or near the privy, that oblation is for Desire or for Wrath. Then, if it is with a heap [of earth], it is for the Rākṣasas.
Now, having sprinkled this remainder of the oblation with water, he should pour it out towards the south with his face turned downwards; that belongs to the Pitṛs.
One should offer oblations into the fire while seated;
one should give to the ancestors while seated, and present the other offerings as they arise.
One should personally carry out these bali offerings for as long as one lives.
Or else another Brahmin [may perform it]; 16.
"The couple themselves" 17—this is the vow of the householder. 18.
"In the evening she is a woman, in the morning a man. 19.
However, one should offer these bali-oblations from all food—whether it be for the ancestors, for a rite of well-being, or for the sake of wealth. 20.
From the sacrifice itself, [the ritual] ceases. 21.
22. If rice and barley are prepared at the same time, one may consider the requirement fulfilled by performing the offering for either one of them.

23. If food is cooked again and again at the same time, one should perform this ritual of the bali-offering only once. 24. If much food is being cooked in various ways within a single household, one should perform this ritual of the bali-offering from the master of the house’s kitchen alone.

But for one for whom this [offering] succeeds first, having performed the fire-rite with what has been set aside, he should give the first portion to a Brāhmaṇa and then eat; or he may eat even the last portion. Moreover, they also cite this: 27.

At the conclusion of this very offering of oblations (*bali-haraṇa*), one may state one's desire; indeed, it comes to pass for him. However, one should personally offer the oblation of grain (*aśasya-bali*) from barley to rice, and from rice to barley; this is the so-called "grain-oblation" (*satvāśasya-bali*).
One indeed becomes long-lived.

When the chaff and the rinsings of rice have been distributed, he should offer a *bali* with the words, "To the waters. That [offering] belongs to Rudra; that belongs to Rudra. 31. Now, regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices: 1. He should fast on the eve of the full moon.
2. He should fast on the eve of the full moon.

Some say [it is] the following day. Now, that day on which the moon is not seen is the new moon (amāvāsyā). The ends of the fortnights are to be observed as fasts; the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed upon.
One sacrifices toward the bright fortnight with the new-moon oblation, and toward the dark fortnight with the full-moon oblation.

That which is the furthest distance between the sun and the moon is the full moon; that which is the closest approach is the new moon. On the day when the moon is not visible at all, one should perform that as the new-moon sacrifice.
Even while it is still visible, the path [of the moon] is sometimes considered traversed;
thus there are three times for the full moon: at twilight, or when it has set and risen, or when it is high in the sky.
Now, on the day when it is full...
This knowledge has its own separate study; one should either study it or cause those who know it to understand the sections from him. 12.

Now, on the day that the Upavasatha occurs, having offered the morning oblation in the forenoon, he smears this sacrificial mound of Agni all around with cow-dung. 13. Then he prepares the fuel-sticks, made either of Khadira or Palāśa wood. 14.

In the absence of *khadira* or *pālāśa* wood, fuel for all forest trees may be used as required, with the exception of *bibhītaka*, *tilvaka*, *bādhaka*, *nīva*, *nimba*, *rājavṛkṛkṣa*, *śālmali*, *aralu*, *udumbara*, *dhittha*, *kovidāra*, and *śleṣmātaka*.
(15) *Kuśa* grass cut at the forked branches is the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). (16) For the ancestors, it is cut near the roots. (17)
In their absence, all kinds of grass except for *śūka*, *tṛṇa*, *śara*, *śīrya*, *balvaja*, *mutava*, *nalada*, and *śuṇṭha* [are used].
(18) [The materials are] clarified butter, or rice for the *sthālīpāka*, or barley, as well as the *caru*-pot, the stirring-spoon, the *sruva*-ladle, and water kept in a protected place.
(19) And those which we shall set forth as secondary alternatives. (20)
On that day he should not go out;
he should come to his house even from afar;
furthermore, he should buy goods from others but not sell them.
He should not be a talkative man (24);
he should speak the truth (25).

Then, having bathed in the afternoon itself, the husband and wife should eat the fast-day meal—whatever may be their desired food—which should be mixed with clarified butter and prepared with skill (26).
Māṇatantavya said: "The human oblation of one who does not eat the fast-day food becomes as if unoffered.
He is powerless, prone to hunger, and undesirable to people; his offspring become more wretched.
But he who eats the fast-day food becomes powerful, free from hunger, desirable to people, and his offspring become more prosperous."
Therefore, whatever they may desire, they should eat on the day of preparation (upavasatha). On that very night, they should sleep on the ground.
Indeed, they should spend that night alternating between staying awake and sleeping, either by means of some historical narrative or by some other means.
But they should indeed feel aversion toward ritual acts that violate the vow. 7.
They say that one who is traveling abroad need not observe the fast. 8.
"The wife's duty consists in the observance of the vow," so it is said. 9.
One may act in whatever way one desires;
in this very manner, the fast-day (upavasatha) of one who has established the sacred fires also occurs,
as well as whatever the traditional scripture (āmnāya) may prescribe.

Then, having offered the morning oblation in the forenoon itself and having circumambulated the fire from the front, he spreads *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward to the south of the fire. Standing to the east of that grass facing west, he grasps a blade of grass from the *brahmāsana* seat with the thumb and the ring finger of his left hand and casts it out toward the eighth direction, which is southwest, saying: "Expelled is Parāvasu! (1.13–14).
Having touched water, he then sits down on the *brahmāsana* seat, saying: "I sit upon the seat of Vasu. (1.15)
Facing the fire, restrained in speech and with palms joined in *añjali*, he should remain seated until the conclusion of the ritual.
(16) He may speak only that which pertains to the successful accomplishment of the sacrifice. (17) He must not utter speech that is unfit for the sacrifice. (18)
If he should speak speech unfit for sacrifice, he should mutter a verse or a sacrificial formula dedicated to Viṣṇu (19).
Or he should simply say, "Obeisance to Viṣṇu" (20).

But if he should desire to perform both—the office of the Hotṛ and the office of the Brahman—he should, according to this same rule, place either a parasol, an upper garment, a water-pot, or a bundle of *darbha* grass upon the Brahman’s seat; having returned by that same path, he may then perform the other duties (21).
Then, having washed the mortar and pestle as well as the winnowing basket, he spreads *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward behind the fire and sets them down.

Then he pours out the sacrificial oblation—either rice or barley—using either a vessel or a *caru*-pot, saying, "I pour thee out, acceptable to [Name]," while pronouncing the name of the deity once; twice silently.
Then, standing behind [the fire] and facing east, he begins to thresh with both hands, right and left.
Regarding the rice grains that have been husked three times, they say: "One should wash them three times for the gods, twice for men, and once for the ancestors.
He should pour the rice grains over the two purifiers placed beneath.
One should cook the sacrificial food like a pot-offering of wholesome grain, stirring it clockwise while it boils.
Having poured clarified butter over the cooked food, removed it from the fire toward the north, one should pour clarified butter over it once more.
Having kindled the fire, one should strew *kuśa* grass around it on all sides—namely, to the east, south, north, and west.
It should be threefold or fivefold on all sides,
thick and composed of an uneven number of layers,
covering the roots with the tips directed toward the east.
Having spread [the grass] behind [the fire], he draws it forward to the south and likewise to the north;
he should make the tips point south and north.
This is the rule for the strewing of grass in all rites involving oblations.
Some also prepare enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *śamī* wood or of *parṇa* leaves (16).
To the north, there is a *praṇītā* ladle full of water (17), or it may be made of *bhava* wood, according to some (18).
Having placed the *sthālīpāka* on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and added fuel to the fire, he prepares the clarified butter—
either ghee, oil, curd, milk, or barley-gruel. Then,
from that very same sacrificial grass, he makes two strainers (*pavitras*) one span (*prādeśa*) long.
Having hidden the herb, he cuts [the blades] with his fingernail, not with a blade, saying: "You two are purifiers belonging to Viṣṇu.

(22) With this [formula], he wipes them with water, saying: "You two are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu. (23) Having cleansed them, he purifies [the ghee] with the two purifiers whose tips point north. (24)

Grasping [the blades] with the two thumbs and the two ring fingers, he purifies them eastward once with the sacrificial formula: "May the god Savitṛ purify you with a flawless purifier, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya," and twice silently.
Then, having sprinkled them with water, he should throw them into the fire.
Then, having placed this clarified butter over the fire, he should remove it toward the north.
Thus is the procedure for the preparation of the clarified butter (ājya).
First comes the clarified butter, then the cooked rice (sthālīpāka).
Having sprinkled water around the fire, he pours the clarified butter into the cooked rice and begins the offering by taking portions with the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa). 28.2–3.
If, however, he should intend to offer that which has already been spread with a base and poured over with clarified butter, he should first offer the two *ājyabhāga* portions.

Having taken four spoonfuls of clarified butter, he should, for the Bhr̥gus, make it fivefold; then, saying "Svāhā to Agni," he should sacrifice on the north side, and saying "Svāhā to Soma," he should sacrifice on the south side, pouring eastward.
Then, having spread a base for the oblation, he cuts off the portion.

If he is one who takes four portions, he takes from the middle and from the eastern half; if he is one who takes five portions, he takes from the middle, from the eastern half, and from the western half.
He pours clarified butter over the portions. He anoints the places from which the portions were taken so that they do not become stale.

One should offer [the oblation] in the center with the formula, "To Agni, svāhā!"—either once or thrice according to this same rule. Then, having spread an underlayer [of clarified butter] for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, one cuts off a portion from the eastern half of the northern half; one should pour over it twice, making the second pouring the more abundant.
If, however, he is one who performs the five-fold cutting, having spread [ghee] twice and having cut [the portions], he should pour ghee over them twice.
He does not smear back the place of the cutting so as to avoid exhausting the essence of the offering.
With the formula, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! he should offer it in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire].
One should offer oblations of clarified butter with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
(15) The insertion of additional offerings takes place before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
(16) In the case of group rites, there is only one sweeping, one fuel-wood, one sacrificial grass, one sprinkling of water, one clarified butter, and the two portions of clarified butter. (17)
Having taken portions from all [the offerings] together, he offers the *sauviṣṭakṛta* oblation only once (18). Having offered it, he should throw this stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) into the fire (19),
or, having washed it and lifted [the remainder] with it, he should eat (20).
"One should not throw the *sruva* ladle [into the fire]," so say some (21).
For one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there should be a *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to Agni at both the New and Full Moon sacrifices (22).
For one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), it should be dedicated either to Agni or to Agni-Soma at the Full Moon sacrifice (23).
On the new moon day, [the oblation] belongs either to Indra, or to Indra-Agni, or to Mahendra.
Alternatively, even for one who has maintained the sacred fires, the oblation at both the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices may belong to Agni alone.
Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire and sprinkled water around it, he performs the rite for the sacrificial site.

Then, taking a handful of *kuśa* grass from that very sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he should thrice dip the tips, the middle parts, and the roots into either the clarified butter or the oblation, saying: "Licking the offered portion, may they enjoy it.

(27) Then, having sprinkled it with water, he should cast it into the fire, saying: "O Rudra, lord of cattle, who moves along the cords, the bull—do not harm our cattle; let this be an offering unto you, svāhā!
(28) This is called the "sacrificial site" (*yajñavāstu*). (29)
Then, having carried this remnant of the oblation out toward the north and having set it aside, he should present it to the Brahman priest.
He should cause him to be satisfied;
for they declare of the sacrifice: "Following the satisfaction of the Brahmin, may I be satisfied."
Now, if he should have any other food prepared, he should then desire to provide a meal for the Brahmins. A full vessel is the sacrificial fee; he should give that to the Brahman priest.

Having filled a cup or a bowl with food—whether prepared or unprepared, or even simply with fruits—they call this the "full vessel" (pūrṇapātra). 7. In the Pākayajñas, the Brahman alone is the single officiating priest (ṛtvij). 8.
In these sacrifices, he himself becomes the Hotṛ. 9.
A full vessel is the minimum sacrificial fee for the *pākayajñas*.
An unlimited amount is the most excellent.
Indeed, Sudās Paijavana, having sacrificed with a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Indra and Agni, gave a hundred thousand [cows].
Now, if one should not find either the sacrificial offering or a priest for the evening and morning oblations in the domestic fire, or for the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices, what should he do?

(13) The morning oblation does not pass beyond the evening oblation, nor does the evening oblation pass beyond the morning oblation; the Full Moon sacrifice does not pass beyond the New Moon sacrifice, nor does the New Moon sacrifice pass beyond the Full Moon sacrifice.
(14) Within this very interval, he should seek to obtain either the sacrificial offering or a priest. (15)
Alternatively, one may cook the fruits or the leaves of only those herbs and trees that are fit for sacrifice and offer them;
indeed, Pākayajña Aiḍa used to say that one should at least offer water as a final resort, for that is truly an offering.
There is an expiation for what has not been offered. 16–18.
"A Brāhmaṇa should not be one who neglects his vows. Furthermore, they also cite this:
"As long as [the sacrifice] has not been offered, he should maintain the continuity of the rite by means of fasting alone."
Now, when he obtains [something], he should offer it as a libation;
in this way, his vow remains continuous. This is the rule for offerings of oblations from this point forward.

At the end of a mantra, there is the utterance of *svāhā*. (25) In offerings of clarified butter (*ājya*), one should offer by taking small portions after having consecrated the clarified butter itself; there are no portions for the *ājyabhāga* deities, nor is there a *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. (26) In offerings of clarified butter where no specific rule is prescribed, the oblation is performed with the *mahāvyāhṛti*s both before and after [the main offering]. (27)
As at the taking of the hand [in marriage], so at the tonsure ceremony, the initiation, and the hair-cutting ceremony;
when the rite has been completed, the singing of the Vāmadevya hymn is for the sake of peace, for the sake of peace.
Thus ends the first chapter.
One should take a wife under an auspicious lunar mansion (1);
she should be one praised for her auspicious marks and chosen by an expert (2);
in the absence of such a woman, one may take [the earth] in morsels (piṇḍas) (3).
From the heart of the altar, from the cow-pen, from the crossroads, from the gambling-ground, from the place where a corpse was burned, and from a salt-flat—these are the [earths] to be gathered;
the ninth is that which is to be brought together from all [these places].
They should be made uniform by having the same characteristic marks.

Placing [the vessel] in his hand, he should cause it to be brought near to the maiden, saying: "Truth indeed is first; no one transgresses Truth. Upon Truth this earth is supported; may all this become that. Having uttered her name, he should say: "Choose one of these.
He should marry her if she chooses one of the first four.
However, some say she may even choose one from among all the vessels.

Having soaked either *klītaka* seeds, barley, or beans in the best of spirits (*surottama*), he should sprinkle her, together with her body, three times on the head, saying: "O Desire, I know thy name; thy name is Intoxication. He should utter the husband's name with the words, "I bring him hither," ending each with *svāhā*. With the next two [verses], he should wash her lap. This is a rite for kinsmen.
At the taking of the hand, fire is placed in a smeared area in front of the hall.
Then, one of the kinsmen, having filled a jar with steady water, accompanied by a water-pot and covered, stands silently in front of the fire, circumambulating it to the south and facing north.
Another [stands] with a goad. They set down in a winnowing basket, behind the fire, parched grains mixed with *śamī* leaves, measuring four handfuls.
And [he should give] a stone for grinding.
Now, she whose hand he is about to take should have her head washed and bathe.
The husband should clothe her in a new garment with the verse, "Those who cut [the wool]," and with the verse, "Clothe her, clothe her with a garment."
While she is veiled and wears the sacrificial cord over her left shoulder, he should lead her forward and recite: "Soma gave her to the Gandharvas... (RV X.85.41).

Behind the fire, while she steps upon a mat woven from *kaṭa* grass, or something similar, or upon her foot, he should cause her to recite: "May the path my husband treads be prepared for me" (RV X.85.23).
If she does not recite it herself, he should recite it on her behalf.
He should bring the edge of the sacrificial grass to the edge of the mat. 22.
To the east, at the edge of the mat, he sits to the south of the bridegroom. 23.
While she maintains contact with his right hand, he offers six oblations of clarified butter with the verses beginning, "May Agni come first. 24.
Having offered oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis individually (25) and collectively (26), they both rise up for the fourth [offering] (26). 1.
The husband, having walked around behind her, stands to the south facing north, taking hold of the bride’s joined palms. 2.
Her mother or her brother, having taken the parched grains, should cause the bride to step upon a stone with her right forefoot. 3.
The one who has taken her hand recites: "Mount this stone. 4.
The brother pours a single handful of parched grains (*lāja*) from his own joined palms into the joined palms of the bride.
She offers it into the fire as a sacrifice, pouring clarified butter over it while keeping her palms unseparated, reciting: "This woman speaks in favor [of the gods].
For the two subsequent verses, she uses: "Aryaman, the god, and Pūṣan... (and so forth).

When the oblation has been offered, the husband, having moved around as he came, circumambulates the fire from left to right; or a Brahmin who knows the mantra [does so] with the verse: "The maiden goes around for the sake of her fathers.

(8) Having been led around, she stands in that same manner, steps across in that same manner, mutters in that same manner, scatters [the grain] in that same manner, and offers the oblation in that same manner.
(9) Thus three times. (10)
Having poured the remainder into the fire with the winnowing basket, they cause [the sacrificer] to step forward toward the north-east with the formula, "One for food.
Having stepped forward with the right foot, he should follow with the left.
He should say, "Do not overstep the right foot with the left."
He should address the onlookers with the mantra: "Auspicious is this bride.
(14) Having walked around the fire from behind, the water-bearer sprinkles the head of the groom and likewise that of the other [the bride] with the verse beginning, "May they anoint them together.

(15) Having taken hold of the joined palms of the bride with his left hand, and having grasped her right hand—palm upturned and including the thumb—with his right hand, he mutters these six verses for the taking of the hand, beginning with, "I take thy hand. (16)
When the [funeral] rites are completed, they carry [the body] toward the north-eastern direction. There, at a distinguished Brāhmaṇa family, the fire has been prepared. 2.

The ground should be level, covered with grass, and free from cracks;

One should predict fear of fire from the *aśvattha*, those prone to death from the *plakṣa*, suffering from weapons from the *nyagrodha*, and eye disease from the *udumbara*.

Having spread out the seat-grass (viṣṭara) with the verse "yā oṣadhīḥ," he should sit down upon it facing north; if there are two, they should each sit separately with their respective verses, placing the other [seat-grass] at their feet.
With the words "O divine waters," he should look at the water;

"Thou art the food of glory; thou art the food of greatness; thou art the food of fortune; bestow fortune upon me"—with these words he should drink three times. The fourth time he should drink silently. Having drunk again until it is full, he should give the remainder to a Brāhmaṇa.

"Except for the sacrifice" (21); "Perform [the rites]" refers to the sacrificial ritual (22);

The teacher, the officiating priest, the graduate, the king, one for whom one has performed a wedding, and a dear guest— these twenty-four should be honored at intervals of a year;
and again at a second sacrifice and a second wedding, and again at a second sacrifice and a second wedding.
